takeaways: A wrong branch prediction flushes the instructions already fetched.
The 2-bit counter moves one step toward the resolved direction.
Prediction is a guess; resolve still happens in EX or MEM.

title: Bus
introduction: A register-transfer machine often time-multiplexes one bus. One driver is valid. Two enabled drivers make X. Nobody driving is Z. Contention is invalid data, not a third numeric value.
guide: Enable one source onto the bus.
Enable two different values — X.
Disable all — Z.
This is the same rule as the CPU internal-bus tab.
takeaways: Two enabled drivers make the bus X.
Contention is invalid data, not a third numeric value.

title: Control Word
introduction: SA, SB, and DA are 3-bit register selects. ALU is 3 bits (000 add, 001 sub, 010 and, 011 or, 100 xor, 101 pass). MB is 0 when the result comes from the ALU. RW is 1 when the destination captures that result on the clock edge.
guide: Select an operation.
Read SA, SB, DA, ALU, MB, and RW.
Select a signal and see which path it enables.
Generate the word and watch the write edge.
takeaways: A control word drives the datapath.
Each field selects a specific function.
Register write happens on the clock edge.

title: Register Transfer
introduction: Move register values through the ALU and watch a shared bus.

title: Transfer
introduction: RTL is an assignment: destination ← source or ALU(source). R3 ← R1 + R2 reads both sources combinationally and writes the sum on the clock. A move copies one register and skips the ALU.
guide: Load values, then step R3 <- R1 + R2.
Try a move without an operator.
Only + - & | ^ are accepted here.
Read which registers changed.
takeaways: A move copies one register and skips the ALU.
The write happens on the step, not while you type.

title: Bidirectional
introduction: A bidirectional register can shift left or right. Direction is a control, not a second clock. Universal registers include this plus hold and load.
guide: Shift right and watch the bits walk.
Switch direction and shift left.
Load a known pattern first so the walk is visible.
Do not change direction mid-bit unless you mean to.
takeaways: Direction is a mux on the neighbor.
Left and right are opposite serial paths.
Hold is neither left nor right.

title: Johnson
introduction: A Johnson (twisted ring) feeds back the inverted last bit. It visits 2N states for N flip-flops: walking 1s then walking 0s. Decoding is simple (two-bit patterns).
guide: Watch 1s fill, then 0s fill.
Count 2N steps for N bits.
Compare with a binary counter's 2^N states.
Use this when you want more states than a ring without a full binary decode.
takeaways: Johnson feeds back the inverted last bit.
States are not binary count; they are a twisted ring.

title: Parallel
introduction: n D flip-flops share CLK and often an Enable. When Enable is 1, the whole word loads on the edge. When 0, the word holds. That is the CPU's register file bit in miniature.
guide: Load a word into the parallel register.
Turn enable off and clock — the word holds.
Turn enable on and clock — the new word appears.
Read binary, hex, and unsigned together.
takeaways: A register is parallel flip-flops sharing a clock.
All bits update on the same edge.

title: PIPO
introduction: Parallel-in parallel-out is the ordinary register: load a word, read a word. Shift modes are off. Same as the parallel tab with the PIPO name used in textbooks.
guide: Load a word.
Clock with hold — it stays.
Read all bits at once.
Treat this as a named synonym for parallel load.
takeaways: No serial walk unless you change mode.
Enable still chooses load versus hold.

title: PISO
introduction: Parallel-in serial-out loads a word, then shifts it out one bit per clock. Transmitters use PISO to send a register on one wire.
guide: Load a parallel word.
Shift and watch the serial pin.
After n clocks the word has left.
Load again to start a new frame.
takeaways: Load then shift is the usual sequence.
One pin carries the whole word over time.

title: Registers
introduction: Parallel load and every shift-register mode.

title: Ring
introduction: A ring is a shift register with the last bit fed to the first. One circulating 1 is a one-hot state. Period is n for n stages if you start with a single 1.
guide: Watch a single 1 circulate.
Count clocks until it returns.
If you start with 0000 it stays dead — load a 1.
Compare with Johnson on the next tab.
takeaways: Feedback is the last bit, not inverted.
A legal ring state is one-hot.
Length is N for N flip-flops.

title: SIPO
introduction: Serial-in parallel-out shifts bits in, then you read all Qs at once. Receivers often use SIPO to assemble a word from a pin.
guide: Shift bits in serially.
Read the parallel word after n clocks.
Compare with SISO: the bits are the same, the ports differ.
Hold by stopping the clock.
takeaways: After n shifts the word is complete.

title: SISO
introduction: Serial-in serial-out shifts one bit per clock. After n clocks, the first bit has walked to the last stage. Use it for delay lines and serial links.
guide: Shift 1011 through SISO.
Clock four times and read the serial output.
Watch each stage take its neighbor.
Reset and send a different nibble.
takeaways: Serial modes move one bit per edge.
Latency is n clocks for an n-bit word.
The bit at Qn is the oldest bit.

title: Universal
introduction: Hold, shift left, shift right, and parallel load in one block, selected by mode bits. It is the textbook 4-function register (74194-style teaching model, not a vendor part).
guide: Switch between hold, shift, and load.
Load 1011, then shift.
Hold for two clocks and confirm no walk.
Change mode only between edges in your mental model.
takeaways: Mode selects hold / left / right / load.
This is a teaching universal register, not a datasheet.

title: Page Table
introduction: Each VPN has an entry: valid, frame, dirty, referenced, and permission bits. A fault means the page is not resident. Loading a page updates the table so the next lookup can succeed.
guide: Set virtual pages, physical frames, and page size.
Enter a virtual address and click Lookup.
Select a VPN and inspect its page-table entry.
A valid bit of 0 is a page fault until you handle it.
Watch the frame highlight follow the selected mapping.
takeaways: The VPN indexes the page-table entry.
The frame number selects the physical page. The offset is copied.

title: Protection
introduction: Each page has read, write, execute, and user/supervisor bits. The lab checks presence, then privilege, then the requested access. A missing page is a page fault. A denied permission is a protection fault.
guide: Enter a virtual address.
Choose Read, Write, or Execute.
Choose User or Kernel.
Read the permission bits for that page.
Observe whether the access is granted or faulted, and why.
takeaways: R, W, X, and user/supervisor bits control the access.
An invalid mapping is a page fault.
A denied permission is a protection fault, not a successful translation.

title: TLB
introduction: The TLB caches recent VPN-to-frame translations, tagged by ASID. A hit skips the page table. A miss walks the table and may install an entry. A page fault is not a TLB miss.
guide: Configure TLB size, associativity, and replacement.
Enter a virtual address and an ASID, then Translate.
See whether the lookup hit, and which entry was used.
Try a thrashing trace and an ASID switch.
takeaways: A hit avoids the page-table walk.
The TLB caches translations, not page data.
ASID keeps one process from using another's translation.

title: Translate
introduction: A virtual address is a page number (VPN) plus an offset. The offset is copied into the physical address. The VPN indexes the page table (or TLB) to find the frame. This lab is not an operating system.
guide: Set the page size (offset bits) and enter a virtual address.
Click Translate to split the address and walk the TLB and page table.
Observe the translation and the resulting physical address.
Try Read and Write, and addresses that miss or fault.
takeaways: The offset stays unchanged. The VPN is translated to a frame.
A TLB hit can bypass the page-table walk.
Page size is 2 to the power of the offset bits you choose.

title: Two-level
introduction: The virtual address splits into a page-directory index, a page-table index, and an offset. Second-level tables exist only for directories that are present. This is a teaching two-level split, not a claim about one processor's page-table depth.
guide: Set directory, table, and offset bits.
Enter a virtual address or load the example.
Read the page-directory index and the page-table index.
Follow the walk from directory to second-level table to frame.
The frame plus the offset is the physical address.
takeaways: The address splits into directory, table, and offset fields.
Unused second-level tables need not exist.
The physical address is the frame shifted by the offset width, plus the offset.

title: CMOS Inverter
introduction: See which transistor pulls the output, and the current while it switches.

questions.question: Halfway between the rails, which transistors conduct?
questions.answer: Both. Both are on in the transition region, which is why crowbar current flows from VDD to ground.

questions.question: With Vin = 0, the output is pulled up by…
questions.answer: The PMOS. A low gate turns the PMOS on and the NMOS off.

questions.question: Static current in a settled CMOS inverter is…
questions.answer: Ideally only leakage. One network is always off in a settled state.

questions.question: Why is the PMOS usually wider?
questions.answer: Holes are slower than electrons. Lower hole mobility is compensated with more width to balance the edges.

title: CMOS NAND Gate
introduction: Parallel PMOS, series NMOS, and a truth table that follows the inputs.

questions.question: For a NAND output to go low, the inputs must be…
questions.answer: All inputs high. The NMOS devices are in series, so every one of them must conduct to reach ground.

questions.question: In a CMOS NAND the PMOS devices are…
questions.answer: In parallel. The pull-up is the dual of the series pull-down.

questions.question: A NAND output is 0 only when…
questions.answer: All inputs are 1. All series NMOS devices must conduct.

questions.question: NAND is usually preferred to NOR because…
questions.answer: Series NMOS is cheaper than series PMOS. Stacking fast NMOS devices costs less than stacking slow PMOS devices.

questions.question: In a CMOS NOR the PMOS devices are…
questions.answer: In series. Parallel NMOS pull-down, series PMOS pull-up.

questions.question: NOR output is 1 only when…
questions.answer: All inputs are 0. Every series PMOS must be on.

questions.question: Wide NOR gates are avoided because…
questions.answer: Series PMOS stacks are slow. Each extra series PMOS adds resistance to an already weak pull-up.

title: CMOS Power Consumption
introduction: Separate dynamic, short-circuit, and leakage power.

questions.question: You double VDD and keep everything else fixed. Dynamic power becomes…
questions.answer: 4×. Dynamic power is α·C·VDD²·f, so doubling VDD quadruples it.

questions.question: Which term does not need switching activity?
questions.answer: Leakage. Leakage flows whenever the supply is on.

questions.question: Raising temperature mainly increases…
questions.answer: Leakage. Subthreshold current grows exponentially with temperature.

questions.question: Halving frequency at fixed VDD halves…
questions.answer: Dynamic power. Dynamic power is proportional to f; energy per switch stays C·VDD².

questions.question: If you make the PMOS much wider, where does VM move?
questions.answer: Toward VDD. A stronger pull-up wins the current balance, so the output stays high until Vin is larger. VM climbs toward VDD.

questions.question: VIL and VIH are where the slope equals…
questions.answer: −1. Unity-gain points bound the region where noise is amplified.

questions.question: NMH is…
questions.answer: VOH − VIH. High noise margin is the gap between the output high level and the input high threshold.

questions.question: Lowering VDD makes the noise margins…
questions.answer: Smaller. Margins scale roughly with the supply.

questions.question: Double the length of a distributed RC wire. Its Elmore delay becomes about…
questions.answer: 4×. Both R and C scale with length, so delay grows with length².

questions.question: Long-wire delay grows with length as…
questions.answer: L². R and C both scale with L.

questions.question: The standard fix for a long wire is…
questions.answer: Insert repeaters. Repeaters split the wire so delay becomes linear in length.

questions.question: The Elmore delay of a lumped RC is…
questions.answer: 0.69RC. 0.69RC is the 50% point of a single-pole response.

questions.answer: VGS > VTH. A gate voltage above threshold inverts the surface and forms an electron channel.

questions.question: Below threshold the device is in…
questions.answer: Cutoff. In cutoff only subthreshold leakage flows.

questions.question: Carriers in an NMOS channel are…
questions.answer: Electrons. NMOS conducts with electrons, which are faster than the holes a PMOS uses.

title: MOSFET I–V Characteristics
introduction: Sweep VGS and VDS and read the square-law curves.

questions.question: In saturation, raising VDS a little mostly…
questions.answer: Leaves the current almost flat. Past the knee the channel pinches off and current is set by VGS, so the curve flattens.

questions.question: The linear and saturation regions meet where…
questions.answer: VDS = VGS − VTH. That is the pinch-off point, the knee of each curve.

questions.question: In the square-law model, saturation current scales with…
questions.answer: (VGS − VTH)². Id,sat = ½·k·(VGS − VTH)².

questions.question: Doubling W (same L) makes the current…
questions.answer: Double. k is proportional to W/L.

questions.question: tpHL depends mainly on…
questions.answer: The NMOS strength. A falling output discharges through the NMOS network.

questions.question: Raising VDD (same load) usually makes the gate…

questions.question: tp is measured between…

questions.question: Setup violations can be fixed by…
questions.answer: Lowering the clock frequency. A longer period gives data more time to arrive.

questions.question: Slack below zero means…
questions.answer: Timing fails. Negative slack is a violation.

title: Addressing Modes
introduction: Effective address = base + index×scale + displacement. Scale is 1, 2, 4, or 8. RIP-relative addressing is common in 64-bit code. LEA computes addresses without a memory access. Segment bases are mostly simplified in long mode.
guide: Choose base, index, scale, and displacement.
See the effective-address math.
Compare RIP-relative addressing.
Execute load and store examples.
takeaways: RIP-relative addressing is common in 64-bit code.
LEA computes addresses without a memory access.
Segment bases are mostly simplified in long mode.

title: Assembler & Disassembler
introduction: Assembly maps to variable-length byte sequences. Labels resolve to relative targets. Disassembly recovers instruction boundaries from bytes. Stepping updates registers, flags, and memory. Intel and AT&T syntaxes differ in notation.
guide: Write Intel-syntax x86-64 code.
Assemble and inspect bytes.
Disassemble bytes back to code.

takeaways: Assembly maps to variable-length byte sequences.
Disassembly recovers instruction boundaries from bytes.
Stepping updates registers, flags, and memory.
Intel and AT&T syntaxes differ in notation.

title: Decode & Datapath
introduction: The front end must find instruction boundaries. Decode translates x86 instructions into internal µOps. Execution units specialize by operation type. Branches redirect fetch when prediction is wrong. Retirement preserves architectural order.

Identify instruction boundaries.
Decode operands and control.
Trace data through execution units.
takeaways: The front end must find instruction boundaries.

title: Instruction Encoding
introduction: Instruction length ranges from 1 to 15 bytes. Prefixes modify operands and addressing. ModR/M selects register and memory operands. SIB encodes scale-index-base addressing. Displacements and immediates extend the instruction.

takeaways: Instruction length ranges from 1 to 15 bytes.
ModR/M selects register and memory operands.
Displacements and immediates extend the instruction.

title: Memory & Cache
introduction: L1 is tiny and fast. L2 and L3 trade capacity for latency. TLBs cache virtual-address translations. Cache lines move blocks, not single bytes. Misses can dominate performance.
guide: Explore L1, L2, L3, and DRAM.
Try cache hits and misses.
Inspect TLB translation.
Measure approximate latency.
takeaways: L2 and L3 trade capacity for latency.
Cache lines move blocks, not single bytes.

title: Micro-operations (µOps)
introduction: One x86 instruction may become multiple µOps. Some simple instructions map to one µOp. Macro-fusion can combine adjacent instructions. Micro-fusion can keep an address and an operation together. A µOp cache can bypass repeated decode.
guide: Select a complex x86 instruction.
See it crack into µOps.
Track dependencies and fusion.
Compare µOp counts.
takeaways: One x86 instruction may become multiple µOps.
Some simple instructions map to one µOp.
Micro-fusion can keep an address and an operation together.
A µOp cache can bypass repeated decode.

title: Out-of-Order Backend
introduction: Register renaming removes false dependencies. Reservation stations hold waiting µOps. The scheduler issues ready work. The ROB tracks program order and retirement. Precise exceptions require in-order retirement.
guide: Rename architectural registers.
Dispatch to reservation stations.
Issue ready µOps out of order.
Retire in program order.
takeaways: The ROB tracks program order and retirement.

title: Overview
introduction: x86 uses variable-length instructions. Complex instructions decode into simpler µOps. Modern cores execute out of order. Large cache hierarchies hide memory latency. x86-64 preserves substantial backward compatibility.

takeaways: Complex instructions decode into simpler µOps.
